DietView

Interactive, hierarchical visualization of predator stomach-content data

Stomach contents are identified to uneven depth: one prey is named to species, the next only to “Teleostei”, and some material cannot be placed at all. DietView keeps all of it. From a long table with one row per prey record, it attaches a taxonomic lineage (from WoRMS, or from a lineage table you supply), keeps every record that stopped at a coarse rank as an explicit unidentified category below that rank, and shows the whole diet at every rank in one sunburst, by prey records or by weight. It also reports the classical frequency of occurrence, how identification depth changes with digestion, and can write the result to a single HTML file that opens in any browser. See the documentation site.

Overview

DietView is built around a single input contract (one row per prey record in a stomach) and one reusable specification object. From there it offers:

  • taxonomy on demand: resolve prey against WoRMS by AphiaID (preferred) or name, following unaccepted names to their valid AphiaID, with exact matching first, then WoRMS TAXAMATCH for misspellings, and a provenance log to review; or join a lineage table for a fully offline, reproducible run;
  • within-rank importance in two currencies (prey records and weight), where every taxonomic rank sums to 100 % and unidentified prey is an explicit NA category rather than a dropped row;
  • covariate stratification by any user-declared columns (period, year, size class, length bins, region, …), plus helpers to derive periods and length bins;
  • a digestion identification-bias diagnostic that shows how the finest resolved rank shifts toward coarse ranks as digestion advances;
  • interactive sunbursts (plotly), with one color per taxon kept the same in every panel, so strata can be compared at a glance;
  • three outputs: a Shiny explorer, a self-contained HTML dashboard (searchable, sortable predator cards, with optional ID photos from iNaturalist or Wikimedia Commons, each credited with its author and license), or plain plotly figures;
  • exploration & reproducible aggregation: sample summaries, prey-accumulation curves for sampling sufficiency, classical per-rank frequency of occurrence, threshold-based aggregation that collapses rare prey upward to a reproducible resolution (pooled, cross-predator, and per-predator), and a sampling-unit by prey-category matrix export for multivariate analysis.

The package ships real, public data to learn on: ices_diet (9,639 prey records from 4,231 stomachs of 22 fish species, North Sea, Skagerrak-Kattegat and Baltic Sea, 2020-2024), ices_stomachs (every sampled stomach, empty ones included) and ices_lineage (their frozen WoRMS classification). Source: ICES Stomach Content Database, ICES, Copenhagen; extract distributed with the R package stomachr (Lindmark 2026). See ?ices_diet.

Installation

DietView is distributed through R-universe:

install.packages("DietView",
  repos = c("https://sosthenea.r-universe.dev", "https://cloud.r-project.org"))

Or install the development version from GitHub:

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("SostheneA/DietView")

Optional features need a few more packages: worrms (WoRMS taxonomy), shiny + DT (interactive app), rmarkdown (self-contained HTML).

install.packages(c("worrms", "shiny", "DT", "rmarkdown"))

Basic use

A minimal, fully offline workflow on the bundled ICES stomach data (a long table of prey records plus a frozen lineage lookup, so no internet is required):

library(DietView)

# 1. base long table: one row per prey record, NO taxonomy columns
#    (drop non-food items and nematodes, which are mostly parasites, not prey)
phylum <- ices_lineage$phylum[match(ices_diet$prey_aphia_id, ices_lineage$prey_aphia_id)]
dat <- ices_diet[ices_diet$item_type != "non_food" & !phylum %in% "Nematoda", ]

# 2. declare column roles once (nothing is hard-coded)
spec <- dv_spec(
  predator       = "predator_common",
  predator_latin = "predator_latin",
  stomach        = "stomach_id",
  prey_id        = "prey_aphia_id",
  prey_name      = "prey_name",
  weight         = "prey_weight_g",
  count          = "prey_count",
  digestion      = "digestion_label",
  covariates     = c("region", "year", "quarter")
)

# 3. attach taxonomy -- offline via a lineage table ...
prep <- dv_prepare(dat, spec, taxonomy = "table", lineage = ices_lineage,
                   verbose = FALSE)

#    ... or live from WoRMS (needs 'worrms' + internet; results are cached):
# prep <- dv_prepare(dat, spec, taxonomy = "worms")

# 4. metrics: within-rank importance (NA included; each rank sums to 100 %)
tree <- dv_tree(prep)
dv_rank_table(tree, "Class")

# 5. figures + digestion diagnostic, here for Atlantic cod
cod <- dv_prepare(dat[dat$predator_common == "Atlantic cod", ], spec,
                  taxonomy = "table", lineage = ices_lineage, verbose = FALSE)
dv_sunburst(dv_tree(cod), mode = "occurrence", title = "Atlantic cod")
dv_digestion_diagnostic(cod, by = "region")

# 6. explore, check sampling sufficiency, aggregate, and export
dv_summary(prep)                                  # stomachs, records, taxa per predator
dv_prey_accumulation(cod, permutations = 50)      # cumulative prey curve
dv_fo_table(cod, rank = "class")                  # classical per-rank %FO

agg  <- dv_aggregate_threshold(cod, threshold = 10)    # prey in < 10 stomachs move up a rank
m    <- dv_matrix(agg, currency = "occurrence")        # set x category matrix (-> vegan)

# 7. write a standalone HTML dashboard (one file, opens in any browser)
dv_deploy(cod, file = "cod_dashboard.html", dir = tempdir(),
          strata = c("region", "quarter"),
          length_col = "length_cm")

# or explore interactively
run_dietview(prep)

See Getting started with DietView for the rendered walk-through.

The explicit-NA philosophy

Where identification stops, or WoRMS has no finer rank, DietView keeps the deeper rank columns as NA and shows them as an explicit “NA” category (white in the sunburst). Two consequences follow:

  • within-rank percentages still sum to 100 %, so nothing is quietly rebased onto the identified fraction only;
  • identification gaps stay visible instead of being hidden inside a functional grouping.

The digestion diagnostic makes this concrete. On real surveys, records identified to species become rarer as digestion advances, and more of them stop at a coarse rank or stay unresolved; the diagnostic shows by how much, instead of hiding it.

Input format

One row = one prey record in one stomach. Column names are free; you map them to DietView roles once via dv_spec(). The bundled ices_diet table is in this format: one row per prey record, with the stomach-level variables (predator, length, haul, region, year, …) repeated on each row, and its lineage lookup is ices_lineage (ICES Stomach Content Database, ICES, Copenhagen; extract distributed with the R package stomachr, Lindmark 2026; see ?ices_diet). The data dictionary (inst/extdata/dietview_data_dictionary.md) also documents the small 24-record example dietview_example.csv (base table) and dietview_example_lineage.csv (lineage lookup), kept for tests and quick checks of the mechanics.

citation("DietView")

Related work

DietView is a visualization and reporting layer; it does not model diet composition or fit selectivity. It complements diet-analysis workflows built on vegan (multivariate community statistics), to which dv_matrix() is the direct bridge, the WoRMS toolchain (worrms), and interactive graphics via plotly and htmlwidgets. The sunburst and dashboard design follow the southern Gulf of St. Lawrence (sGSL) diet dashboard it generalizes.
